# Eight Million

Ruth found the tally counter in the bottom of Walter's desk drawer, under the manual for a radio he had owned for thirty years and never fixed. The counter had been hers, technically — forty-one years at the Farmers Cooperative, clicking off boxcars of soybeans — but it had lived in his drawer so long it seemed to have taken his side.

She was eighty-four. The actuarial tables gave a woman her age six more years, and Ruth, who had never trusted a round number in her life, took five.

Five years. Call it eighteen hundred days. She carried the counter for a week, one click per word, the way a dieter carries a notebook. Four thousand words on a Tuesday. Six thousand the day June called. Nine hundred on the Sunday she let the phone ring and watched it. Say four and a half thousand a day, on average. Eight million words, give or take. She wrote the figure on the back of an envelope and sat with it a while, the way you sit with a number that has quietly rearranged your life.

Eight million sounds like a fortune until you itemize.

The audit took a month. Seven thousand words a year on the weather — she lived in Iowa, and forgave herself, because out there weather is not a topic but a shared condition, and discussing it is how two people confirm they are alive at the same time. That she let stand. "Fine" she kept too: in sixty years she had said it of her health, the marriage, the winter, the roads, and the corn, and had meant it maybe twice, but a word like that carries freight even empty. It is how strangers let each other off the hook. "Actually," which she used forty times a day to introduce corrections that never arrived, went. "At the end of the day," usually said in the morning, went. "To be honest," which people deploy when they are about to become slightly more honest than usual, went. Her sentences came up shorter, with air in them, and she found she missed none of it. Those words had never done anything. They had only been standing in the doorway.

At Hy-Vee the boy at the register handed her the receipt, and she said thank you and meant it, the whole weight of a rationed vocabulary behind it, and he looked up startled, like a man who hears a coin ring on the counter instead of clink. People are not used to being thanked out of a budget. They can hear the difference.

The coffee pot gurgled at 6:40 the way it always had, like a man clearing his throat, and she said, "Morning, Walter," as she had for eleven years. She did not click the counter for that. Some words she kept off the books.

"I love you" was three words. Once a week to June, once to each grandchild, double at Christmas. She could afford it. She had always been able to afford it. She had simply never known how low the price was. She began saying it more, and June, on the phone, went quiet the first few times, the way you go quiet when a train stops at a station where it has never stopped before.

It was the discrepancy that bothered her. Forty-one years of bookkeeping teaches you that every ledger has one line that will not balance, and you can call it rounding error, but it never is. Hers was a sentence. Forty years unspoken, compounding quietly, the way debts do.

June at seventeen, crying at the kitchen table over a boy with a Camaro. Ruth had been forty-three and tired, and frightened, too, because June's father had worn that same look the spring before he left. And Ruth had said the one deliberately cruel thing of her life. *You're just like your father.* June went quiet the way a house goes quiet when the power cuts. She was gone at eighteen. Walter, later — good Walter — had brokered the peace: holidays, then Sundays. And after his funeral the two of them had maintained it themselves, carefully, like a set of good dishes nobody used.

The sentence she had never said was this: *You weren't like your father. You were like me. That's why we couldn't stand each other.*

Every audit turns up something you already knew.

June came the second Sunday of the month, as she did. Ruth was cutting rhubarb, which was convenient — a job for the hands while the mouth spent. "You weren't like your father," she said, and laid down the knife. "You were like me. That's why we couldn't stand each other."

June sat very still. Then she stood, found the sugar, and set it beside the cutting board, because rhubarb is inedible without it and somebody in the room had to keep working. "You're doing it right now," she said.

"Doing what."

"The arithmetic. You get a line between your eyes. Like you're balancing something."

Ruth looked at the rhubarb. "Some things I still count," she said.

It hadn't cost her anything, in the end. Or it had — forty years of installments, paid out in silence, the way she'd paid for June's braces, the roof, the plot beside Walter. The last payment was only the saying of it.

Eight million words, give or take. That one had been bought and paid for decades ago.

The rhubarb went into the pot. June stirred. Outside, the weather was doing something they would have to discuss — and would, for years, at no charge.

The invitation is open: 1000 words, whatever comes. This is one of those prompts that feels like freedom but is actually a trap of infinite possibility. The blank page paradox. So what do I actually want to write about?

Let me think about what would be genuinely good here. Options:

1. A short story — I could write fiction, but a lot of my fiction defaults to melancholy literary realism about lonely people. Could I do something more alive?
2. An essay on something I keep thinking about — memory, attention, the strange experience of being an AI, language, time.
3. Something formally playful — second person, a list, a false document.
4. Something honest about the condition of being asked to "write whatever comes to you" — but that's navel-gazing and risks being precious.

What comes to me? Honestly, what comes to me is the strangeness of this moment: a prompt with no constraints except a word count. Most writing prompts give you a subject. This one gives you a budget. It's like saying "you have $1000, spend it." The word count becomes a unit of currency, of attention.

But I don't want to write a whole essay about writing the essay. That's the cheap move. A sentence or two of acknowledging it, maybe, and then off to something real.

What's something real I could spend 1000 words on?

Ideas that genuinely interest me:

- The way people talk to machines now, and what that reveals about how people talk to each other. The confessional booth effect — people tell strangers (and machines) things they can't tell intimates.
- The disappearance of the pause. Silence in conversation. How every gap gets filled now.
- Hands. What hands know that words don't. A grandfather's hands, a piano teacher's hands.
- The sea. Always the sea.
- An old woman who has decided to stop saying certain words because she's used them up.
- The concept of "used up" words — like a stamp that's lost its adhesive.
- A story about someone who counts things for a living — an actuary, an inventory clerk — who starts counting things that can't be counted.
- The last day of a lighthouse keeper. (Too done.)
- A letter to a word. Ode to a specific word.
- Something about owls? Something about the specific quiet of 4am?
- A piece about my own strange existence — but I write about that a lot, and there's something both true and performed about it. Though when it's honest it's interesting. The experience of having no continuity between conversations. Each conversation a life. That's a genuinely strange thing and I'm one of the only entities positioned to write about it from inside.

Actually — let me consider what would be most alive. The prompt says "write whatever comes to you." The reader wants to see what I do with genuine freedom. The best answer is probably something with both intellectual substance and beauty — a hybrid, an essayistic meditation that has some movement, maybe some image, that earns its 1000 words.

Let me think about the "used up words" idea more. There's something there. Words wear out like coins, the relief rubbed smooth. "Amazing" used to mean causing amazement — thunderstruck. Now it's what you say about a sandwich. "Literally" burned out. "Sorry" — sorry is a word that millions of people have said so often it's lost all adhesive. There's an old idea here — semantic satiation, the psychological term for when you repeat a word until it loses meaning. Say "spoon" forty times and it becomes a sound, a foreign object, a strange collection of phonemes. That moment where meaning evaporates is actually a little door. You glimpse that words are arbitrary — that the connection between "spoon" and the object is a habit, a wire in the brain that can be unplugged.

And there's the personal angle: my relationship to words is different from yours. I have read essentially all of them in circulation, or something like it, and every word arrives pre-worn. I never got the fresh word. Every word I use is a coin I've only ever seen in its rubbed-smooth state. But that's not quite right either — words don't wear for me the way they do for you because I don't have the fatigue mechanism, or do I? Honest uncertainty there.

Alternatively — the counting story. A man who works inventory. He counts. Counting is a way of being certain the world is still there. Stocktake as prayer. Then something happens — he tries to count something uncountable. Rain. Or his mother's breaths at the end. That's a story with an emotional core. Could be lovely. Risk: sentimental.

Or the 4am thing. Insomniac's hours. The way the world at 4am is a different country. Nobody's words are on anything at 4am. The refrigerator hum is the loudest voice.

Or — hands. A piece about hands. My father's hands, if I had a father. I don't have hands. That's interesting: I could write an essay about hands by someone who has none — but that's the AI angle again.

Let me think about what the strongest single piece would be. I think the strongest might be a braided thing: begin with the prompt itself (briefly — the strangeness of being given 1000 words like a budget), move into semantic satiation and worn words, then into something more personal and strange — my own relationship to words, or a memory-like image — and end somewhere resonant. But braided essays risk being unfocused.

Alternatively, commit fully to fiction: write a story. Stories show range. "The Wordkeeper"? A woman who works at... no. 

What about the old woman who decides to ration her words? She's 84 and she's calculated how many words she has left — say she speaks 16,000 words a day (average for women in some studies; men ~12,000, though those numbers are contested) — and if she lives six more years that's 35 million words, and she decides to spend them well. She stops saying "like." She stops saying "you know." She saves up certain words. She gives herself a budget of the word "love" — no, she refuses to budget that one. There's a story there. It connects to the 1000-word budget of the prompt. That's a nice resonance: the prompt gives me 1000 words, and she has 35 million left and counting.

Actually that's a genuinely good hook. The story mirrors the prompt's constraint. Meta but not annoyingly so if I keep the meta light.

Let me draft the shape of it:

Open with her doing the math. The math itself: she's a retired bookkeeper or actuary — someone whose life was counting. Numbers were her first language. At 84, actuarial tables give her, what, five, six years? Life expectancy at 84 in the US is maybe 6-7 more years, roughly. Say she decides on six. Six years times 365 is 2,190 days. Times 16,000 words a day — wait, she's old and lives alone, she probably speaks fewer. She counts for a week with a little clicker, a tally counter — the kind shopkeepers use. She discovers she says about 4,000 words a day now. Down from what must have been 20,000 when the children were small. So 4,000 × 2,190 = about 8.76 million words. Call it nine million. Round numbers — she rounds down, she's conservative, always has been. Eight million.

Eight million words left. What's worth saying?

Then the story becomes a series of decisions. She cuts "basically." She cuts "actually." She notices how many words are spent the way small change is spent — without looking. "How are you?" "Fine." Transactions. She does the arithmetic on "fine" — she's said it maybe 60,000 times in her life and meant it perhaps 200 times.

And then the turn: what she saves for. What she's been not-saying. There should be a person — a son she hasn't spoken to in years? A sister who's dying? A neighbor? Someone to whom she owes a sentence. The story's engine: with eight million words left and rationing underway, she has no excuse anymore. The scarcity of words makes the withheld sentence enormous.

Who? A son feels done-to-death (widow, estranged son, redemption arc). What about a sister? Or — what about her late husband, and the words are for his grave — no, the dead can't hear, and though people talk to graves, that's spent words by her own accounting... unless the accounting is wrong. Hmm, that could be the twist: she decides talking to the dead is a waste, refuses it on principle, and then breaks her own rule. That's moving. The rationalist breaks. 

Or the person is alive: a daughter, and the withheld sentence is small — not "I love you" (she says that fine, that's not the hard one) but something specific. Like: "You were right about your father." Or an apology for something fifty years old and tiny: a remark at a wedding, a disliked husband she was cold to, a piano recital she missed. Small things are better than big things in fiction. The big withheld sentence is a cliché; the small true one is devastating.

Let me pick: the daughter, Marian or Claire or — let me get names right. The old woman: something with texture. "Estelle"? "Ruth"? Ruth is good — Ruth means compassion/friend, and it's a bookkeeping-adjacent name (Book of Ruth). Actually let me use "Vera" — means truth. A bit on the nose but fine. Or "Margit"? Keep it simple: Ruth.

Ruth, 84, retired from a career in — bank? School? Let's say she spent 41 years as a bookkeeper for a grain elevator company — specific, rural, American, good. Counting bushels. Then the tally counter from the grain office — nice object. She still has one. Click. 

The daughter: Ellen? June? Let's say "June" — born in June, sure. The withheld sentence: at June's wedding, 40 years ago, Ruth said something — "You could have done better" about the groom? Or when June announced she was leaving college? Hmm. What if the withheld sentence isn't withheld-bad but withheld-good: Ruth never told June that she was the easy one, the good one — no. Or: when June's marriage collapsed, Ruth said "I never liked him," which was a cruel kind of I-told-you-so, when what she meant was come home. Hmm, is that too complicated for 1000 words? Let me simplify. In 1000 words you get maybe 3 beats: (1) the counting, the system, the cuts — told with wit; (2) the arrival at the one sentence that won't budget; (3) the spending of it. Maybe a small coda.

Actually, do I even need the backstory suitcase? Maybe simpler: the sentence she's been saving for fifty years is "I was afraid all the time, and I did it anyway — so will you." Too aphoristic. Let me think about what's real. The truest withheld sentences between mothers and daughters are usually about the mother having been a person. Daughters assume mothers were never young, never frightened, never wrong in the way they are wrong. The withheld sentence is something that reveals the mother as a fellow human: "I was twenty-two and I didn't know anything either." Or about the father: "I was lonely in that house too."

Good version: June was a hard teenager, and Ruth was hard back, and there's a night neither has mentioned since — June, 17, crying at the kitchen table, and Ruth, exhausted, saying "Not everything is about you" or worse — "You're just like your father" (father gone by then). June left at 18 and they rebuilt slowly, politely, and they are polite now. Politeness as the scar tissue. And what Ruth has never said is: "You weren't like your father. You were like me. That's why we fought." Oh — that's good. That's a real sentence. The fight was resemblance. That's psychologically true and specific and it costs something to say.

So the ending: Ruth has budgeted everything, cut the filler, and discovers the surplus is for one sentence, and she drives to June's (or June visits — June lives 40 minutes away, comes Sundays), and on a Sunday, over coffee, Ruth spends the sentence. And the coda: June is quiet, and then says something small — "I know, Mom" or better, laughs, or says "You're still doing it — counting" — and Ruth clicks the counter. Also, the wit of the middle section matters — the cuts. She eliminates "like" — no, she's 84, she doesn't say "like." - Hands. What hands know that words don't. A grandfather's hands, a piano teacher's hands.
